quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [The Missing Invoice] Rosa, the accountant, spent Tuesday morning re-sorting the filing cabinet and complaining about the new coffee machine. After lunch she asked the courier for the delivery record for 14 March. On Wednesday she asked Mr. Vane, twice, whether he had "definitely" sent the invoice, and offered to resend it herself.
quests.question: What is Rosa most likely concerned about?
options: Whether Mr. Vane is qualified to send invoices without another employee checking them.
Whether the client has paid the invoice on time.
Whether the courier has been charging the company too much for deliveries.
Whether the invoice actually reached the client.
quests.correctAnswer: Whether the invoice actually reached the client.
quests.hint: Ignore the details that do not connect to the invoice, then follow the questions she asks.
quests.explanation: The cabinet and coffee machine are background. Rosa asks for a delivery record, asks twice whether the invoice was sent, and offers to resend it. All point to doubt about whether it arrived.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Design Team Update] At Monday's meeting, Ms. Abara praised the design team's speed. Mr. Grieg, sitting beside her, called it "admirable," then asked how many revisions had been needed. Later he mentioned to Ms. Abara that the client had "commented on some inconsistencies."
quests.question: What is Mr. Grieg's main aim?
options: To congratulate the design team without the client's comments.
To suggest that the revisions were caused by the client's changes.
To suggest that quality may be a problem behind the speed.
To ask for a longer deadline for the client's next project.
quests.correctAnswer: To suggest that quality may be a problem behind the speed.
quests.hint: Follow his remarks in the order he makes them.
quests.explanation: He accepts the praise, then asks about revisions, and later raises the client's comments about inconsistencies. Together, the questions point to a concern about quality.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Sixty-Two Percent] The council says the town centre car park is "well used," with average occupancy of 62 percent. Shop owners say that on Saturdays, when they most need customers, the car park is full by eleven and half empty by three.
quests.question: What does the 62 percent figure leave out?
options: It suggests that the car park is never busy on weekdays.
It hides differences between busy and quiet times.
It shows that the car park is too large for the town.
It proves that shoppers prefer to park elsewhere.
quests.correctAnswer: It hides differences between busy and quiet times.
quests.hint: What does an average combine, and what do shop owners describe?
quests.explanation: An average mixes very busy and very quiet periods. The shop owners describe a Saturday pattern that the figure does not show.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Details] Lucas said yes to organising the charity quiz, then asked whether Katya could "help with the details." At the second planning meeting he brought slides for the first half only. When Katya offered to take the rest, he said, "That would be a relief," and glanced at the clock.
quests.question: What does Lucas's behaviour show?
options: He is losing interest in the charity that the quiz supports.
He took on more than he can manage.
He wants Katya to take over the whole quiz.
He is planning the second half in a more detailed way.
quests.correctAnswer: He took on more than he can manage.
quests.hint: Track what he asks for at each stage.
quests.explanation: He asks for help early, prepares only half, and is relieved when Katya offers to do the rest. Each step shows he is overstretched.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [The Café Across the Street] Tessa's competitor, the café across the street, posted congratulations on her award. It added: "We look forward to seeing what she does next. We are sure she will be busy." Within a week the rival had put her signature pastry on its own menu.
quests.question: What does the rival's action show about its post?
options: The rival is publicly gracious but competing by copying.
The rival is genuinely delighted for Tessa and is copying out of respect.
The rival is angry about the award and wants to hide it.
The rival is warning Tessa that it will compete on price.
quests.correctAnswer: The rival is publicly gracious but competing by copying.
quests.hint: Compare the public message with the rival's action a week later.
quests.explanation: The post is polite. However, adding her pastry to their menu shows the rival is competing with her.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [If It Would Help] When the board asked whether he would chair the review, Dr. Osei said, "If it would help." He then asked about the timetable, the budget, and whether the report would be published in full.
quests.question: What does Dr. Osei want before agreeing?
options: He wants to be sure that the board will read the report.
He is interested in the salary and expects to be paid for it.
He is willing, but wants assurance that his work will not be limited.
He does not want to chair the review, but cannot refuse.
quests.correctAnswer: He is willing, but wants assurance that his work will not be limited.
quests.hint: What do his three questions have in common?
quests.explanation: Each question concerns the conditions of the work, and the last one is about whether the results will be fully published. He wants guarantees before he agrees.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Friday Evening] The company's statement on the safety review was sent at 5:47 p.m. on the Friday before a public holiday. It was four sentences long and linked to a sixty-page report.
quests.question: What does the company's timing suggest about its aims?
options: It considers the safety review too minor to explain properly.
It has written the statement in a hurry before the holiday.
It wants as many people as possible to read the report.
It would prefer the news to attract little attention.
quests.correctAnswer: It would prefer the news to attract little attention.
quests.hint: What do the timing and length of the statement suggest?
quests.explanation: Sending news late before a holiday, with a short message pointing to a long report, is a way to reduce attention.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [In the Spring] In January the landlord promised to replace the windows "in the spring." In April he sent a leaflet on "keeping heating costs down." In June he raised the service charge, citing "ongoing improvements."
quests.question: What has happened to the promised windows?
options: The landlord has lowered heating costs, and the windows are no longer needed.
The windows were replaced in spring, and the charge covers the cost.
The windows have not been replaced, and his communications avoid the issue.
The tenants have asked the landlord to delay the work.
quests.correctAnswer: The windows have not been replaced, and his communications avoid the issue.
quests.hint: Compare his promise with what he sends later.
quests.explanation: The promise is followed by a leaflet about heating costs and a charge for improvements. Nothing says the windows were done.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Lowest in Six Years] The minister said unemployment among young people has "fallen to its lowest level in six years." The figures also show that the number of young people in full-time education rose by 8 percent over the same period.
quests.question: Why might the fall in youth unemployment be misleading?
options: More young people have left the country to look for work.
The fall is due to a rise in the number of jobs for young people.
The figure is false, since education numbers are counted separately.
Part of the fall may be due to more young people studying, not more finding work.
quests.correctAnswer: Part of the fall may be due to more young people studying, not more finding work.
quests.hint: What else changed over the same six years?
quests.explanation: Students are usually not counted as unemployed. A rise in education could reduce unemployment without more jobs.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Guest Speaker] The guest speaker did not mention the college's name once, addressed the students as "you all," and answered questions with "as I said earlier." She left before the reception began.
quests.question: How engaged was the speaker with the college?
options: She wanted to avoid the reception because of a previous disagreement.
She was not particularly engaged with this audience.
She was delighted to visit the college and had prepared for it.
She was nervous and rushed to leave after the questions.
quests.correctAnswer: She was not particularly engaged with this audience.
quests.hint: Which details show personal connection, and which are missing?
quests.explanation: She never named the college, used general address, and left early. These are signs of little engagement.
clueWords: did not mention the college's name

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [For When Things Calm Down] Marit gave her colleague a wrapped book on time management, with a note: "For when things calm down." The colleague, who had just missed a deadline, said "Thank you" and put it in her drawer.
quests.question: How might the colleague have received the gift?
options: Marit was hoping to borrow the book back in a week.
The gift could be read as a criticism.
The colleague was grateful and will read the book at once.
The colleague felt that the gift showed Marit's respect for her.
quests.correctAnswer: The gift could be read as a criticism.
quests.hint: Consider the topic of the book alongside the colleague's recent situation.
quests.explanation: A book on time management, given right after a missed deadline, may seem like a hint. The colleague's brief thanks and the drawer suggest she took it that way.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Greatest Weakness] Asked about his greatest weakness, the applicant said, "I care too much about details." Asked for an example, he described a time he had "stayed until midnight to fix a misplaced comma."
quests.question: What kind of answer did the applicant give?
options: He is giving a rehearsed answer that presents a strength as a weakness.
He is careless and has to check his work many times.
He is nervous and cannot think of a real example.
He has a serious weakness that he prefers not to discuss.
quests.correctAnswer: He is giving a rehearsed answer that presents a strength as a weakness.
quests.hint: Would a real weakness be described this way?
quests.explanation: Caring about details is usually a strength, and his example makes him look diligent. The answer avoids a genuine weakness.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Original Price] A shop advertised its jackets at half price. The "original" price was in small type on the tag. A customer noticed that on the shop's website the same jackets had never been listed at that price.
quests.question: What might be wrong with the "original" price?
options: The "original" price may have been inflated to make the discount look bigger.
The customer misread the small type on the tag.
The website has been updated to remove the original price.
The jackets were always sold at a low price in the shop.
quests.correctAnswer: The "original" price may have been inflated to make the discount look bigger.
quests.hint: What does the website show about the earlier price?
quests.explanation: If the higher price never appeared online, the discount may not be a real reduction.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Two Witnesses] Witness A says the cyclist "came out of nowhere." Witness B, standing further along the road, says the driver "was looking at his phone." Neither says what the cyclist was doing before.
quests.question: Which statement is best supported?
options: Witness B is more reliable because he was standing further along.
The accounts do not contradict each other, but neither gives the whole picture.
The driver is at fault, since he was looking at his phone.
Witness A is lying because he cannot describe what the cyclist did.
quests.correctAnswer: The accounts do not contradict each other, but neither gives the whole picture.
quests.hint: Ask whether both statements could be true at once.
quests.explanation: One describes the cyclist's appearance, the other the driver's attention. Both could be true. Neither describes the earlier moments.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Lively Presence] In this term's report, Enzo's teacher wrote, "Enzo is a lively presence in class." Last term she had written, "Enzo participates well and completes his work."
quests.question: What has changed between the two reports?
options: Enzo has become disruptive, and his teacher chose a gentler word for it.
Enzo has a new teacher who values different qualities.
Enzo has stayed sociable, but his work may have become less consistent.
Enzo is now doing better work but is quieter in class.
quests.correctAnswer: Enzo has stayed sociable, but his work may have become less consistent.
quests.hint: What was praised last term, and what is missing this term?
quests.explanation: "Completes his work" has disappeared, and "lively presence" describes personality, not achievement. The change hints at a decline in work.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Unexpected Issues] The builder's first estimate was "about £8,000." After work began, he mentioned "unexpected issues" with the wall, then "additional materials." The final bill was £11,500. His invoice thanked the client for "understanding."
quests.question: What does the growing bill suggest about the estimate?
options: The builder charged less than the estimate for the extra materials.
The wall was new, so the issues were unavoidable.
The estimate was low or incomplete, and the builder assumes the client will accept.
The client asked for extra work, which explains the higher bill.
quests.correctAnswer: The estimate was low or incomplete, and the builder assumes the client will accept.
quests.hint: Follow the phrases the builder uses as the price rises.
quests.explanation: The estimate was far below the bill, and each new phrase justified a rise. The final "understanding" assumes acceptance.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Offline] In the meeting, Pia proposed a new schedule. Two colleagues said they "liked the thinking." Nobody asked a question. The manager wrote something down and said, "Let's pick this up offline."
quests.question: What has the meeting decided about the proposal?
options: The proposal has been neither accepted nor rejected, and there is little enthusiasm.
The manager has approved the proposal and wants to discuss details privately.
Pia has probably been asked to rewrite the schedule before the next meeting.
The colleagues have rejected the proposal, but politely.
quests.correctAnswer: The proposal has been neither accepted nor rejected, and there is little enthusiasm.
quests.hint: What did colleagues do after hearing the proposal?
quests.explanation: "Liked the thinking" is polite. No questions were asked and the discussion was postponed. That suggests limited interest.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Exciting Changes] This month's newsletter announced "exciting changes" to parking arrangements. The details are on page 6. Page 6 says that visitor permits will now cost £3 a day, described as "a small contribution towards maintenance."
quests.question: Why are the changes called "exciting"?
options: The changes are exciting because they reduce parking fees for residents.
The changes are optional, and visitors can choose to pay.
"Exciting changes" is used to soften the announcement of a new charge.
The permits will cost less than before the changes.
quests.correctAnswer: "Exciting changes" is used to soften the announcement of a new charge.
quests.hint: Compare the headline word with what page 6 says.
quests.explanation: The exciting changes turn out to be a new fee. The wording is chosen to make the news sound better.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Front Desk] The hotel replied to a review: "We are sorry you found the noise disruptive. Our records show you did not report this during your stay." The reviewer's original comment had said, "The front desk was closed when I tried."
quests.question: What does the hotel's reply fail to address?
options: The hotel's reply defends itself but does not answer the reviewer's claim.
The hotel accepts that the desk was closed and apologises for it.
The hotel has fixed the problem and thanks the reviewer for the report.
The reviewer stayed at another hotel and has confused the two.
quests.correctAnswer: The hotel's reply defends itself but does not answer the reviewer's claim.
quests.hint: What did the reviewer say prevented a report, and does the hotel address it?
quests.explanation: The hotel says no report was made, but the reviewer says the desk was closed. The reply ignores that explanation.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Three Pounds] "For £3 a month you can help a child get an education." The advert shows a smiling child in a spotless uniform. In small print: "Your donation supports our programmes generally. It is not allocated to individual children."
quests.question: What is misleading about the advert?
options: The charity keeps the £3 for its own staff.
Each donor is matched with a child and receives letters from him.
The child in the advert is the one who receives the donation.
The advert suggests a personal link that the small print does not support.
quests.correctAnswer: The advert suggests a personal link that the small print does not support.
quests.hint: Compare the large message with the small print.
quests.explanation: "Help a child" and the photo imply a direct link. The small print states the donation supports general programmes.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Not Aware] "We did not know about the problem," the director said. Two emails, released later, showed that a manager had reported the problem to his office in March.
quests.question: How do the emails affect the director's claim?
options: The director knew about the problem but forgot to mention it.
The director is telling the truth, because the emails were sent to another office.
His statement is contradicted by the emails.
The emails prove that the manager was responsible for the problem.
quests.correctAnswer: His statement is contradicted by the emails.
quests.hint: Compare the director's claim with the release.
quests.explanation: If a report was sent to his office in March, his claim to have not known is at least questionable.
clueWords: did not know about the problem
reported the problem to his office

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [The Blurb] The publisher's blurb calls the memoir "a searingly honest account." The final chapter covers the author's years abroad in one paragraph. The reviews quoted on the cover all come from writers published by the same company.
quests.question: How reliable is the book's praise?
options: The blurb is honest, since the memoir has been praised by independent critics.
The reviewers are experts who work for rival publishers.
The praise is fair, but the author should have written more about her travels.
The praise may not be independent, and the account is not fully complete.
quests.correctAnswer: The praise may not be independent, and the account is not fully complete.
quests.hint: Who is doing the praising, and what is treated briefly?
quests.explanation: The blurb and cover reviews come from within the company, so they are not independent. One paragraph for years abroad suggests gaps.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Transformation] The gym's "transformation" posters show three members and "results in 12 weeks." The small print says: "Results vary. Featured members also followed a personalised nutrition plan (additional cost)."
quests.question: What did the featured members' results depend on?
options: The results vary because each member trains for a different number of weeks.
The featured members were paid by the gym to appear in the posters.
The results probably depended on a paid extra as well as the gym membership.
The results came from the gym alone, and the nutrition plan was free.
quests.correctAnswer: The results probably depended on a paid extra as well as the gym membership.
quests.hint: What did the featured members do besides go to the gym?
quests.explanation: The small print says featured members also paid for a nutrition plan. So the poster credits the gym for a result that included another purchase.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Five Thousand] The campaign says "5,000 residents oppose the plan." The petition was open online to anyone, and the last 2,000 signatures arrived in a single day from addresses outside the borough.
quests.question: What does the campaign's number overstate?
options: The number overstates opposition among local residents.
The number is too low because many residents did not know about the petition.
The campaign counted signatures from people who live in the borough.
The number is accurate because each signature was checked.
quests.correctAnswer: The number overstates opposition among local residents.
quests.hint: How many signatures may not be residents?
quests.explanation: About 2,000 of 5,000 came from outside the borough, so the figure does not represent residents.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Ready in Thirty Minutes] The blogger says the pie is "ready in 30 minutes." The ingredients list includes "pre-cooked chicken" and "ready-made pastry." Several readers comment that it took them "almost two hours" from scratch.
quests.question: Why did readers take longer than thirty minutes?
options: The readers did not follow the recipe correctly.
The blogger's time is accurate for anyone who follows the recipe carefully.
The pie needs a long time in the oven, which the blogger left out.
The thirty minutes leaves out preparation steps that some readers had to do.
quests.correctAnswer: The thirty minutes leaves out preparation steps that some readers had to do.
quests.hint: What does the thirty minutes assume about the ingredients?
quests.explanation: The time depends on cooked chicken and ready-made pastry. Readers who made everything took much longer.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [In Line] The chairman told shareholders that profits were "in line with expectations." Two lines later he noted that "expectations were revised in October."
quests.question: How might profits be "in line" with expectations?
options: Profits may be in line only because expectations were lowered.
Profits exceeded the original expectations by a small amount.
The chairman is confused about the difference between profits and expectations.
Expectations were raised in October because profits had improved.
quests.correctAnswer: Profits may be in line only because expectations were lowered.
quests.hint: What happened to the expectations before the report?
quests.explanation: Being "in line" depends on what was expected. A revision before the result could mean the target moved to fit.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [More Than Last Year] The school raised £4,200 at the fair. Organisers said this was "more than last year." Last year's total was £4,150, and this year's fair had two extra stalls.
quests.question: How impressive is the school's result?
options: The extra stalls lost money, which explains the small rise.
The increase is very small, given the extra stalls.
The result is impressive, because the fair earned much more per stall.
The organisers exaggerated by saying it was more than last year.
quests.correctAnswer: The increase is very small, given the extra stalls.
quests.hint: Compare the totals, and consider the extra stalls.
quests.explanation: The rise is £50. With two more stalls, the gain is disappointing, even though "more" is true.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [The Majority] Councillor Reyes thanked "the many residents who shared their views." He said the decision to approve the plan "reflects the majority of responses." The published summary shows 412 responses, of which 231 opposed the plan.
quests.question: How does the councillor's claim compare with the figures?
options: He is describing the residents who were consulted in person, not by post.
His claim does not match the published figures.
The published summary is wrong, because the responses were counted twice.
His claim matches the figures, since most residents supported the plan.
quests.correctAnswer: His claim does not match the published figures.
quests.hint: Compare the claim with the numbers.
quests.explanation: Of 412 responses, 231 opposed the plan, which is a majority. Approving the plan cannot reflect that majority.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [In Stock] The retailer's site said "in stock." After the order it said "preparing." Four days later it said "dispatch soon." The customer service agent said, "The system shows the item as available."
quests.question: What do the repeated messages suggest about the stock?
options: The customer has changed the order, which explains the delay.
The item is ready to be sent and will arrive within a day.
The agent has checked the warehouse and confirmed the item is available.
The stock information may be unreliable.
quests.correctAnswer: The stock information may be unreliable.
quests.hint: Compare the agent's words with four days of waiting.
quests.explanation: "Available" is repeated by the system while nothing ships. This suggests the stock data may be wrong.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct inference.
quests.passage: [Front Row] Mr. Feng's leaving speech thanked the students for "keeping him young" and the staff for "their patience." He did not mention the headteacher, who sat in the front row.
quests.question: What might the omission of the headteacher mean?
options: He was thanking only the people who had worked with him longest.
The headteacher had asked him not to mention her.
He forgot the headteacher, who arrived after the speech began.
The omission may be deliberate and may point to tension.
quests.correctAnswer: The omission may be deliberate and may point to tension.
quests.hint: Who is thanked, and who is missing?
quests.explanation: He thanks two groups but not the person in the front row. Such an omission can signal tension, though the passage does not state it.
